claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
The hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10 contains local phase variations.
Dense-grid nanoindentation can capture the local elastic response of distinct microstructural regions.
Dense-grid nanoindentation can capture the local yield response of distinct microstructural regions.
FIB-milled micro-cantilever bending tests can characterize local elastic and yield behavior in HfNbTiVAl10.
Local mechanical tests can identify potential crack-initiation zones.
Multiscale chemical fluctuations and local phase variations mediate the relationship between local mechanical properties and bulk behavior.
An effective-medium or homogenization model calibrated using local measurements can predict bulk Young's modulus.
An effective-medium or homogenization model calibrated using local measurements can predict bulk yield strength.
Local testing and effective-medium homogenization can predict an indirect measure of bulk toughness.
The proposed method can directly link microscopic heterogeneity to macroscopic toughness and strength.
Predicted Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness will be within 10–15% of tensile and fracture-test measurements.
The proposed process will be approximately five to ten times more efficient than full-scale iterative CALPHAD, first-principles, and machine-learning methods.
The method may become unreliable when sampled local regions do not represent the material's microstructural heterogeneity.
The method may become unreliable if local tests fail to capture critical crack-propagation phenomena.
The method may become unreliable at high strain rates.
The method may become unreliable at elevated temperatures.
Fracture toughness is less reliably inferred from local tests than elastic and yield responses because crack nucleation and propagation may not be fully represented.
